page.text:
The theory of series provides the microscopic analytical lens of complex
analysis. While the geometric viewpoint of Augustin-Louis Cauchy and
Bernhard Riemann emphasizes paths, potentials, and conformal
transformations, Karl Weierstrass built complex analysis entirely upon
the foundation of convergent power series and analytic continuation.

These two seemingly disparate perspectives merge in complete harmony.
Within any disk contained in its domain of definition, every holomorphic
function is analytic: it expands into an absolutely and uniformly
convergent Taylor series whose coefficients are dictated by its complex
derivatives or Cauchy contour integrals.

When an analytic function encounters an isolated point where it fails to
be defined—an *isolated singularity*—the Taylor series is superseded by
the *Laurent series*, which incorporates both positive and negative
powers of $(z - z_0)$. The negative powers form the *principal part*,
which measures the exact algebraic obstruction to extending the function
across the singularity. The coefficient of $(z - z_0)^{-1}$ is the
*residue*, which compresses the global topological loop integral into a
single local number.
